context:
Start with a correction, because it is the most useful thing this page can offer. The two measures in this site's tracked list for Arkansas, Senate Resolution 7 and House Resolution 1013 from the 2026 fiscal session, are not artificial intelligence bills. Both are identically titled resolutions authorizing introduction of a nonappropriation bill to amend the requirements for a digital asset mining business and the authority of local governments over such businesses. Neither mentions artificial intelligence. They are keyword false positives, swept in because cryptocurrency mining and data center policy share vocabulary with AI infrastructure policy, and both died at sine die adjournment on 29 April 2026. Arkansas holds a short fiscal session in even numbered years, which limits what can be introduced, so the near empty 2026 record is expected.

The real legislative activity happened in the 2025 regular session of the 95th General Assembly, where Arkansas enacted five AI laws in a single year. Act 159 extends publicity and likeness rights to cover AI created images, voice simulations and likenesses, restricting commercial use of a person's identifiable attributes without consent. Act 827 addresses deepfake visual material of a sexual nature and creates the criminal offense of unlawful distribution of deepfake visual material. Act 977 criminalizes creating, possessing and distributing AI generated child sexual abuse material that appears indistinguishable from a real child, with carve outs for law enforcement and legitimate research. Act 848 requires public entities to adopt formal policies governing artificial intelligence and automated decision tools, with human oversight requirements, employee training and public accessibility. Act 927 settles ownership of generative AI output, providing that the person supplying the inputs owns the result unless the work is created within employment, in which case the employer owns it. Taken together this is a coherent package covering identity, sexual exploitation, government use and intellectual property, and it is broader than what most states produced in the same year.

Arkansas has no comprehensive consumer data privacy act. The general statutes that reach AI conduct are the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act at Title 4 Chapter 88 of the Arkansas Code, which prohibits deceptive and unconscionable practices in business and gives the Attorney General investigative and enforcement authority, and the state's Personal Information Protection Act, which requires reasonable security for personal information and notification when it is breached. Neither mentions artificial intelligence. Both apply to an AI vendor that overstates its product, misrepresents automated decisions, or loses control of the personal data it trained on or collected.

Attorney General Tim Griffin has been more visible on artificial intelligence than most of his peers, though visibility is not the same as enforcement. On 13 January 2026 he created a Senior Advisor for AI role and appointed Deputy General Counsel Kevin Lee to it, with a remit covering training for law enforcement and the legal community, work with agencies and academic institutions on investigative tools, and identifying emerging risks from AI misuse. In May 2026 his office ran an Emerging Issues Series event on AI in legal practice that drew more than 400 registrants. On the federal question he has been direct, joining thirty nine other attorneys general in opposing the proposed ten year federal moratorium on state AI regulation and publicly welcoming its removal from federal legislation on 1 July 2025. He has also joined a 54 attorney general coalition urging Congress to establish an expert commission on AI and child exploitation. No formal Arkansas AI enforcement action against a company has been identified.

reading.body:
Arkansas passed five AI laws in 2025, then produced no AI legislation in its 2026 fiscal session. The two 2026 measures tracked as AI bills, SR7 and HR1013, are digital asset mining resolutions that never mention artificial intelligence.

The 2025 package is coherent rather than scattered. Act 159 covers likeness and voice, Act 827 covers sexual deepfakes, Act 977 covers AI-generated child sexual abuse material, Act 848 requires public entities to adopt AI and automated decision tool policies with human oversight, and Act 927 assigns ownership of generative output to whoever supplied the inputs, or to the employer when created within employment. That is identity, exploitation, government use and intellectual property addressed in one session, which is broader than most states managed in the same year.

The 2026 emptiness is structural, not a signal about Arkansas's appetite for AI rules. Even-numbered years bring a short fiscal session with narrow introduction rules, and the two resolutions that did appear were procedural authorizations for a nonappropriation bill, both dead at sine die on 29 April 2026. The state also has no comprehensive consumer privacy act, so the statutes that would reach an AI vendor are the Deceptive Trade Practices Act and the Personal Information Protection Act, neither of which names AI.

Enforcement is the gap. Attorney General Tim Griffin created a Senior Advisor for AI role in January 2026, ran an event drawing more than 400 registrants in May 2026, and joined multistate coalitions opposing a federal moratorium on state AI regulation and urging a congressional commission on AI and child exploitation. No formal Arkansas AI enforcement action against a company has been identified. The record shows legislative activity and executive attention, not adjudication, and it says nothing about the data centers, power contracts or computing buildout that would connect this state's AI story to the grid.

Arkansas's 2025 package regulates conduct by category rather than by technology. Act 159, Act 827 and Act 977 each attach to a harm that already had a legal name, likeness, sexual exploitation, child abuse material, and extend it to synthetic production. Act 848 and Act 927 attach to institutions and ownership instead. The result is that an AI developer in Arkansas faces no general AI statute, only the specific prohibition that matches what the system produces or who it belongs to.

The enforcement machinery is thinner than the legislative output. The Attorney General's AI work in 2026 consists of a staff role, a training event and multistate sign-on letters, all of which shape what enforcers know and what Congress might do. None of it produces a defendant. The Deceptive Trade Practices Act and the Personal Information Protection Act remain the only general statutes that could reach an AI vendor, and both reach it through conduct that predates AI, which means a case would be built on misrepresentation or a data breach rather than on the model itself.

The 2026 fiscal session cannot be read as a verdict on AI policy. Arkansas holds short even-year sessions with narrow introduction rules, and the only two measures tracked here were procedural resolutions authorizing a nonappropriation bill about digital asset mining. Both died at sine die on 29 April 2026. The absence of AI bills in that window reflects the calendar, not a change in position.

What did Arkansas actually pass on AI in 2025?
Five laws: Act 159 on likeness and voice, Act 827 on sexual deepfakes, Act 977 on AI-generated child sexual abuse material, Act 848 on public entity AI and automated decision tool policies, and Act 927 on ownership of generative output.

Are SR7 and HR1013 AI bills?
No. Both are identically titled resolutions authorizing introduction of a nonappropriation bill to amend requirements for a digital asset mining business and local government authority over such businesses. Neither mentions artificial intelligence.

Does Arkansas have a comprehensive consumer data privacy law that covers AI?
No. The state has no comprehensive consumer privacy act. The Deceptive Trade Practices Act and the Personal Information Protection Act are the general statutes that could reach an AI vendor, and neither names AI.

Has Arkansas taken any AI enforcement action against a company?
No formal Arkansas AI enforcement action against a company has been identified in the data.

Who owns the output of a generative AI system under Arkansas law?
Act 927 provides that the person supplying the inputs owns the result, unless the work is created within employment, in which case the employer owns it.

What does the data say about Arkansas data centers, power contracts or computing buildout?
Nothing. The data contains no information on Arkansas data centers, electricity contracts or computing capacity, so it cannot connect the state's AI record to the grid.
